author: zicokolter
text: I should also mention one potential _positive_ consequence of desk-rejects, beyond reviewer load: it requires ACs to interact more meaningfully with papers before the discussion period. I still have my objections, but since it's here to stay for now, I'm hoping for the best.

author: zicokolter
text: @RaiaHadsell This is awesome. If it had already been mentioned, I admit I missed it. Thanks for discussing the topic at length, despite the fact that I'm sure it was already settled.

author: zicokolter
text: @RaiaHadsell I hope so. I would be very happy to be wrong about this. Any chance we could let through a small random sample of desk-rejected papers to test the false reject rate?  Otherwise, there's little way to know.

author: zicokolter
text: @RaiaHadsell @NeurIPSConf I understand it would likely introduce an extremely high logistical burden at this point.  Thanks for considering.  I'm still nervous that this will notably dampen apparent inclusivity of the conference, though.  And isn't all of this an experiment? (not meant negatively) 😀

author: zicokolter
text: @evgeniyzhe I hope it pans out that way.  I'm suspicious that this amount of filtering will notably improve the quality of the reviews.  But on the other hand, the same world conditions making me hope ACs would willingly take on more work, might also just make the reviews better.

author: zicokolter
text: @thegautamkamath @NeurIPSConf Agreed.  I'm just genuinely skeptical of the ability of ACs to make a large number of quick decisions at a threshold that will make this worth the downsides.  And I'm mainly suggesting this in light of current circumstances, which will make these decisions even harsher.

author: zicokolter
text: I'm an AC for NeurIPS, and with ~18 papers, I'd need to desk reject around 3. I'd happily take the three additional weeks we save and offer to be a normal reviewer for 9 papers, if it means we can avoid desk rejects, providing feedback for those with the least experience. n/n

author: zicokolter
text: Desk rejects make sense in journals, where time frames are slower, but I can't see them being fair given the fast turnaround needed for conference publications.  Maybe with a 5% rate, but no way at 20%.  Despite good intentions, in my opinion they were a disaster at IJCAI. 5/n

author: zicokolter
text: To be clear, I'm not talking about rejects for formatting violations, lack of anonymization, etc. We already have mechanisms for desk rejecting those, it just doesn't happen as much as one would think.  A 20% target desk reject rate will mean reasonable papers get rejected. 4/n

author: zicokolter
text: It's extremely discouraging for authors who put in a lot of effort and submitted good work to get a desk reject. _I_ was frustrated about getting one at IJCAI, so I can only imagine how disheartening this is for junior researchers. 3/n

author: zicokolter
text: The main goal of reviews, of course, is to determine which papers get into the conference. But reviewing also provides an extremely useful way for authors to get feedback on their work. If recent ICML meta-reviews are any indication, ACs won't all do a great job with this. 2/n

author: zicokolter
text: The @NeurIPSConf chairs have done a wonderful job managing many unforeseen circumstances, and have my deepest thanks. But in the name of inclusivity, and _because_ they have been so responsive, I want to ask: could we consider killing the desk-reject experiment this year? 1/n
